General Principles
Lateral and medial elbow enthesopathy (commonly referred to as epicondylitis) refers to pain
and tenderness at the lateral or medial epicondyle, respectively, that lasts longer than a simple
strain or sprain.
Medial and lateral elbow enthesopathy are idiopathic conditions that typically are symptomatic
in patients aged 35 to 65 years.
Tissue removed at the time of surgical débridement demonstrates myxoid degeneration
(disorganized collagen without cross-linking and increased extracellular matrix) and
cartilaginous metaplasia. No inflammatory or reparative cells are present.1
Symptoms are associated with activities that use the involved muscles.
Most patients with medial or lateral epicondylitis achieve sufficient symptom improvement
with nonsurgical treatment or no treatment.
Misconceptions about enthesopathy are common and associated with greater symptoms and
incapability.
Practitioners must ensure that patients considering surgical treatment properly understand
enthesopathy, the postoperative recovery, and the evidence that surgical treatment may not
outperform simulated surgical treatment.
Lateral Elbow Enthesopathy (Epicondylitis)
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Lateral elbow enthesopathy (commonly referred to as epicondylitis) is a degenerative change
at the origin (enthesis) of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) muscle at the lateral
epicondyle.
Although work relatedness often is claimed for enthesopathies, no experimental evidence has
documented causation by work (or other) activities.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
In brief, exacerbation is a temporary worsening of symptoms that are expected to return
to baseline because no new or worsened pathology is present, whereas aggravation
implies a new and permanent change or pathology. In certain patients in whom

under a work claim, even if surgeons abide by the evidence that the condition is an
idiopathic enthesopathy of middle age. No evidence exists for activity or work-related
causation nor aggravation.
Epidemiology
Lateral elbow enthesopathy is the most common cause of elbow pain in the general
population.

Epidemiology
In a population-based study overseen by occupational health physicians, an interview
and examination of 4,698 individuals aged 30 to 64 years in Finland was conducted by
trained non-specialists who made a possible diagnosis based on elbow pain in the past
30 days and tenderness over the medial or lateral elbow. Self-reported pain and pain
with resisted wrist extension (lateral) or wrist flexion (medial) was classified as a definite
diagnosis. In this study, 2.8% of individuals were diagnosed as having possible lateral
epicondylitis, and 1.3% of individuals were diagnosed as having definite lateral
epicondylitis; 1.9% of individuals were diagnosed as having possible medial epicondylitis,
0.4% of individuals were diagnosed as having definite medial epicondylitis; and 1.2% of
individuals were diagnosed as having possible or definite lateral and medial
epicondylitis. Medial and lateral epicondylitis had a peak prevalence in individuals aged
45 to 64 years. Several factors were associated with epicondylitis, including smoking and
physical load factors. Possible or definite lateral and medial epicondylitis diagnoses were
more frequent in women; this difference was not noted in a sub-analysis of patients with
definite lateral epicondylitis. The co-diagnosis of medial and lateral elbow enthesopathy
was much higher than that reported in specialist practices, suggesting that many of
these individuals with elbow pain may not have met a specialist’s criteria for diagnosis.
Regardless, these population-based data demonstrate that elbow symptoms are
common in middle age, particularly among individuals who are active at work.2

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Muscles and Tendons
The pathologic changes associated with lateral epicondylitis are localized to the origin of the
ECRB (Figure 1).
The ECRB and the extensor digitorum communis are tendinous near their origin and lie deep
to the extensor carpi radialis longus, which has a more proximal muscle belly.
The common extensors lie superficial to the lateral collateral ligament complex proximally and
to the supinator distally.
The origin of the ECRB lies just superficial to the joint capsule, the location at which it is
accessible via elbow arthroscopy.
The attachment of the ECRB is a diamond-shaped area (approximately 13- × 7-mm area)
superior to the center of the epicondyle.
Figure 1 Illustrations of an elbow show the anatomy of the common extensor tendon. A, With the
capsule removed, the anatomic relationships of the common extensor tendon can be visualized.
B, Intra-articular perspective of the common extensor tendon insertion on the lateral humeral
epicondyle. C = capitellum, ECRB = extensor carpi radialis brevis, ECRL = extensor carpi radialis
longus, ECU = extensor carpi ulnaris, EDC = extensor digitorum communis, RH = radial head.
(Reproduced from Baker CL Jr: Arthroscopic release for lateral epicondylitis, in Yamaguchi K, King

Joints and Ligaments
The ECRB lies directly over the anterior half of the radiocapitellar joint. The lateral ulnar
collateral ligament (LUCL) originates from the center of the epicondyle, and its course is
posterior to the midpoint of the capitellum. Straying posterior to this midpoint places the
ligament origin at risk during débridement of the epicondyle (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustration of an elbow shows the safe zone for débridement during the management of
lateral epicondylitis. The safe zone is defined by an area superior to the dashed line bisecting the
radial head. (Adapted with permission from Smith AM, Castle JA, Ruch DS: Arthroscopic resection
of the common extensor origin: Anatomic considerations. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2003;12[4]:375-
379.)

Patient History
The onset of symptoms typically is atraumatic.
However, symptoms often are ascribed to an event or activity.
Use of the involved muscle may provoke symptoms and often is misinterpreted as causing or
worsening the condition.
The point of maximum tenderness can be localized by many patients to the anterodistal
aspect of the lateral epicondyle, the origin of the ECRB muscle.
Pain often is described as more diffuse, with occasional radiation to the forearm.
Maneuvers that elicit symptoms include any activity that uses or stretches the ECRB, including
passive maximal wrist flexion with the elbow fully extended lifting an objective with the palm
down (often referred to as the chair-lift test), a firm grip, and hitting a backhand in racquet
sports.
Physical Examination
Discrete tenderness to palpation at the anterodistal aspect of the lateral epicondyle (origin of
the ECRB)
Resisted wrist extension with the forearm pronated and the elbow extended is painful.
Passive wrist flexion in pronation and elbow extension is painful.
Lifting with the forearm pronated (palm down, using the wrist extensors) and the elbow
extended reproduces lateral elbow pain; lifting with the forearm supinated (palm up, using the
wrist flexors) is less painful.
LUCL insufficiency can be elicited via the chair sign (Figure 3) or the push-up test (Figure 4).

Evaluation for intra-articular sources of pain
Radiocapitellar arthritis or osteochondritis dissecans often are accompanied by decreased
elbow motion.
Passive flexion of the elbow in pronation and supination may elicit pain and palpable clicking
of a posterolateral plica.
Intra-articular injection of local anesthetic medication may relieve pain.
In patients without focal tenderness at the ECRB origin, physical examination of the cervical
spine, including the Spurling test, is considered because C6 radiculopathy may cause lateral
arm and elbow discomfort.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs are not necessary for diagnosis and rarely alter management.3
Radiographs may be considered if the diagnosis is unclear and if diminished passive elbow
motion is present.
A study of routine radiographs among individuals presenting for specialty management of
lateral epicondylitis revealed calcifications at the lateral epicondyle in approximately one-half
of the individuals and another insertion point ossification or calcification, or osteophytes, in
approximately one-third of the individuals. None of these findings influenced management or
patient outcomes.4
Radiographs may be helpful if complications, such as posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI),
occur after previous management (Video 1).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Signal changes of the origin of the ECRB (thinning or thickening, edema, and occasionally a
defect) are observed on the MRIs of as many as 90% of patients. Similar findings also are
observed on the MRIs of 14% to 54% of patients with an asymptomatic elbow.5 The prevalence
of similar findings in asymptomatic elbows increases with patient age and suggests that more
than 1 in 7 individuals may have imaging study findings of enthesopathy in their lifetime.6
MRI findings do not correlate with symptom severity and they should not be used as an
indication for surgical management.
MRI is not necessary for the diagnosis of lateral epicondylitis but may be helpful in evaluation
for suspected alternative sources of lateral elbow pain (eg, intra-articular pathology, LUCL
insufficiency).
Ultrasonography
The diseased ECRB tendon appears thickened and hypoechoic on ultrasonographic images.
Because ultrasonography is operator dependent, sensitivity and specificity vary.SEND FEEDBACK

Ultrasonography is most useful in the evaluation of lateral epicondylitis if performed by an
experienced operator who uses the imaging modality regularly to diagnose epicondylitis.
Other Studies
Electromyography and nerve conduction study generally are not helpful in the evaluation of
lateral elbow pain. Radial tunnel syndrome is a debated syndrome characterized by pain
without any specific objectively verifiable motor weakness, sensory loss, or changes on
diagnostic tests. Electrodiagnostic testing is, by definition, normal in patients with radial tunnel
syndrome.
Histology
Histologic findings of tissue removed at the time of surgical management of lateral
epicondylitis show myxoid degeneration (collagen disorganization and increased extracellular
matrix), vascular hyperplasia, and cartilaginous metaplasia.
No inflammatory changes (macrophages or neutrophils) and no signs of healing or repair are
observed.
Electron microscopic images show altered cross-sectional diameter of collagen fibers (larger
and smaller), with lack of extracellular cross-linkage and matrix disarray.
Differential Diagnosis for Lateral Elbow and Forearm Pain
Posterolateral plica
PLRI/LUCL insufficiency
Radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve compression)
Occult fracture
Cervical radiculopathy
Capitellar osteochondritis dissecans
Triceps tendinitis
Radiocapitellar osteoarthritis
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Contraindications

Trauma meriting consideration of surgical management
Techniques/Procedures
No scientific or expert consensus exists regarding the management of lateral epicondylitis.7
Many treatment options may offer symptom mitigation by making symptoms less intense or
decreasing the duration of symptoms and allow patients to continue to perform vocational
and avocational activities and improve quality of life during recovery.
Therefore, appropriate treatment options for lateral epicondylitis, other than supportive
management, is a topic of discussion.
The most frequently prescribed nonsurgical treatment options include simple stretches and
isometric strengthening exercises, NSAIDs or acetaminophen, topical nitroglycerin patches, or
a wrist or counterforce brace.
No evidence shows that any nonsurgical treatment option outperforms observation or a
placebo. Although randomized trials occasionally report positive findings, the quality, weight,
and consistency of the findings are limited.8,9
The role of physical therapist oversight of exercises is unclear.
Injections
To date, no injections consistently and meaningfully outperform simulated injection in high-
quality experiments, including corticosteroids, autologous blood, platelet-rich plasma,
concentrated glucose, and botulinum toxin, among others.
In some studies, corticosteroid injection is associated with poorer results after 1 year
compared with simulated injections.
Corticosteroid injections are associated with the risk for skin atrophy and depigmentation.
Botulinum toxin, extracorporeal shock wave therapy, acupuncture, and iontophoresis have
been suggested but are not supported by high-quality experimental evidence.
Outcomes
Many patients become asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic.
Many patients’ symptoms are minimal enough to not seek additional treatment.
Symptoms from enthesopathy almost always resolve without management.
Whether a very small subset of patients exists in whom symptoms do not resolve remains
unclear.


Nonsurgical Management
Whether enthesopathy persists for a lifetime without management is an important topic
of debate. Patients seeking care have concerns regarding persistent enthesopathy;
however, and such concerns usually are inaccurate. Such misconceptions are strong and
consistent contributors to symptom intensity and magnitude of limitations. Surgeons
should be mindful of the potential harms associated with patients selecting treatment
options based on misconceptions and that are inconsistent with their values.
A 1983 study in a rheumatologic setting followed 125 patients, some prospectively and
some retrospectively, for 1 to 5 years and emphasized that 42% of the patients had
intermittent discomfort. Ten of 65 patients and 5 of 65 patients who were evaluated
based on the medical record (retrospective) remained in treatment for 2 years and 5
years, respectively, with symptoms. Continued pain or fear of recurrent pain caused
many patients to change their occupation or cease their hobby or sports activity.10
Conversely, most clinical trials document complete or near-complete resolution of
symptoms for most patients within 1 year regardless of management.
Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical treatment may be considered if patients are dissatisfied with persistent symptoms
after 9 to 12 months.
Contraindications
Given that enthesopathy routinely takes approximately 1 year to resolve, surgeons should
ensure that patients are not electing to undergo surgical treatment based on the common
misconception that recovery is taking too long to resolve or that the pathology will not resolve
without surgical management.
Techniques/Procedures

Surgical Approaches
Open management (Figure 5)
The common extensor origin is sharply incised. The extensor carpi radialis longus muscle is
elevated off the ECRB, which is located deep and slightly posterior to the extensor carpi
radialis longus.
Disorganized tissue (myxoid degeneration) is identified and excised.
The epicondyle may be decorticated.
If the capsule is breached, it can be repaired or left open. A very small risk of fistula
formation exists if the capsule is left open; however, during arthroscopic débridement, the
capsule is routinely débrided and left open.
Side-to-side closure of the superficial tendon
Reattachment of the tendon to the epicondyle with the use of a suture passed through bone
tunnels or a suture anchor is an option.

Arthroscopic management (Video 2)
Advocates of arthroscopic management suggest it allows for increased visualization and
better ability to manage intra-articular pathology; however, whether such pathology is
common or benefits from management is a subject of debate.
The ECRB is located just superficial to the capsule and, therefore, can be débrided by exiting
the lateral capsule and then encountering the ECRB.
The lateral capsule must be resected no more posterior than the midradial head to avoid
LUCL injury.
The origin of the ECRB is released to the point at which the muscle tissue begins.
The usual neurovascular risks of elbow arthroscopy are present (Figure 6).
Denervation (transection of the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm branches with
implantation into the triceps) is untested compared with simulated denervation and should be
considered experimental.

Complications
Pain and Patient Dissatisfaction
As many as 40% of patients experience some level of continued pain.
Instability
The LUCL is located deep and posterior to the origin of the ECRB. If the surgeon strays too far
posterior during débridement or if an excessive amount of the lateral epicondyle is removed
the LUCL origin may be injured, resulting in elbow instability (PLRI).
Stiffness
Any surgical procedure on the elbow may result in stiffness, particularly if combined with intra-
articular procedures.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy

More common with arthroscopic release
Other Complications
Heterotopic ossification around the epicondyle
Infection
Rehabilitation
Hand and shoulder motion are initiated immediately.
If the origin is not reattached, fewer restrictions are necessary.
If restrictions are considered
Postoperative elbow immobilization for the first 1 to 2 weeks postoperatively
Elbow and wrist motion are initiated on discontinuation of immobilization.
A wrist splint can be used for comfort initially.
Extensor stretching can be initiated 3 weeks postoperatively.
Use of the arm for forceful activities can be initiated at 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively.
Gradual increase in activities, including lifting, sports, and functional activities, continues from
6 weeks postoperatively until complete recovery.
Outcomes
Results of surgical management
Uncontrolled series report improvement in most patients who undergo surgical treatment;
however, residual symptoms are reported in 24% of patients 1 year postoperatively.11
A randomized trial comparing open management and simulated open management
demonstrated no difference at any point.12
Uncontrolled series on arthroscopic management are comparable with those on open
management: 93% to 100% of patients are categorized as better or much better at a mean
follow-up of 2 years. Regardless, 20% to 38% of patients continue to have persistent lateral
elbow pain.
A recent randomized clinical trial showed no difference between open and arthroscopic
management of lateral epicondylitis.13
A systematic review comparing open and arthroscopic management demonstrated no
difference in return to work, complication rates, or patient satisfaction; however, a greater

Surgical time is shorter with open management.15
Pearls and Pitfalls
No evidence shows that any treatment option can alter the natural history of enthesopathy.
Surgical treatment is uncommon if patient misconceptions are adequately reoriented and
stress is alleviated. For example, patients may have the misconception that they cannot be
healthy with residual elbow pain. Given that many patients have residual elbow pain
postoperatively, reorientation of this misconception is important before offering patients
surgical treatment.
Loss of patience may motivate some patients to consider surgical treatment. They should
understand that injury (including surgical treatment, which is a controlled injury) improves for
1 year and that many patients have residual symptoms for more than 1 year.
Familiarity with the anatomy of the LUCL and its relationship to the epicondyle, radial head,
and ECRB origin helps surgeons avoid iatrogenic PLRI.
Medial Elbow Enthesopathy (Epicondylitis)
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Medial epicondylitis is much less studied than lateral epicondylitis.
Medial epicondylitis is a degenerative process of the flexor-pronator origin.
Activities that worsen symptoms may seem causative, but the condition is idiopathic.
Epidemiology
Medial epicondylitis is a much less common reason for patients to seek treatment compared
with lateral epicondylitis (ratio, 1:10), but it is otherwise similar in epidemiology.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Neural Anatomy
The ulnar nerve lies just posterior to the medial epicondyle.

The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs just anterior to the medial intermuscular
septum, then divides and runs over the flexor-pronator musculature.
Joints and Ligaments
The anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament is deep to the pronator teres and the flexor
carpi radialis and is the primary valgus stabilizer of the elbow.
Muscles and Tendons 
The common flexor-pronator enthesis is the confluence of five muscles (Figure 7).
Pronator teres
Flexor carpi radialis
Flexor carpi ulnaris
Flexor digitorum superficialis
Palmaris longus
This enthesis originates from the medial epicondyle, the anteromedial joint capsule, and the
anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament (MCL).
Medial epicondylitis most commonly affects the origins of the pronator teres and the flexor
carpi radialis.
In consideration of the differential diagnosis, the medial head of the triceps may be large or
hypertrophied, causing it to snap over the medial epicondyle.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Medial elbow enthesopathy is one of the idiopathic enthesopathies of middle age.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Diagnosis is established based on patient history and physical examination.
Symptoms may be noted with use of the involved muscles.
Pain and tenderness are localized to the medial epicondyle.
A history of numbness or tingling in the ulnar digits suggests ulnar neuropathy, which may
coexist with medial epicondylitis or be an alternative source of symptoms.
Any history of trauma to the elbow should be documented.
Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation is noted slightly anterior and distal to the medial epicondyle, over the
origins of the pronator teres and the flexor carpi radialis.
Resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation elicit a patient’s usual pain.
Flexor-pronator issues in throwing athletes are beyond the scope of this lesson. If the
characteristic symptoms and signs of medial epicondylitis are not present and the patient is a
throwing athlete or has a history of elbow injury, MCL should be examined for insufficiency.16
Examination for snapping medial triceps
The elbow is flexed and extended. The triceps is inspected and palpated for snapping over
the medial epicondyle. This may occur in isolation or in conjunction with ulnar nerve
snapping.
Neurovascular Examination
Examination for cubital tunnel syndrome

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Imaging studies are not obtained unless loss of passive motion is present or other concerns
suggest an additional or alternative pathology.
Radiographs typically appear normal.
As many as 25% of patients may have calcification of the common flexor tendon or the MCL
(Figure 10).
Stress radiographs may be useful in patients in whom MCL insufficiency is suspected.
Posteromedial osteophytes and joint space narrowing may signal valgus extension overload
syndrome.17

Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Ultrasonography
MRIs often are obtained but typically add little to the diagnosis. MRI may be considered in
patients in whom alternative pathologies are suspected. MRI findings must correlate with
patient symptoms because a high rate of changes suggestive of medial epicondylitis may be
observed in patients without symptoms.
Signal changes in the flexor-pronator origin (peritendinous soft-tissue edema, thickening, and
increased signal intensity of the flexor-pronator mass on T1- and T2-weighted MRIs) can be
observed (Figure 11).
Ultrasonography may reveal hypoechoic areas consistent with tendinosis. Ultrasonography is
highly operator dependent, which may substantially influence diagnostic accuracy.18

Other Studies
Electromyography/nerve conduction velocity studies are useful in patients with prominent
symptoms of numbness or signs of ulnar nerve dysfunction on physical examination.
Electrodiagnostic studies are not performed in patients with pain, which is more characteristic
of medial elbow enthesopathy.
Histology
Similar to other enthesopathies, the histopathology of medial epicondylitis is mucoid
degeneration.
Differential Diagnosis
Ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency
Cubital tunnel syndrome and/or ulnar nerve instability
Primary symptom is numbness in the ring and little fingers.

Medial elbow pain may occur in patients with C6 and/or C7 radiculopathy.19
C8 radiculopathy may cause pain along the medial elbow and forearm; however, this typically

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of medial epicondylitis is similar to that of lateral epicondylitis, with
the exception that the proximity of the ulnar nerve, which causes many surgeons to avoid
injections. If an injection is performed, the ulnar nerve must be identified and protected.15
Surgical Management
Indications/Contraindications
Similar to those for lateral epicondylitis
Techniques/Procedures
Surgical Approaches
The incision is centered just anterior and distal to the medial epicondyle, with protection of the
medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve; however, if concomitant ulnar nerve surgery is planned,
the incision is made more posteriorly.
The ulnar nerve should be identified and protected because it runs posterior to the medial
epicondyle. If substantial ulnar nerve symptoms exist preoperatively, decompression or
transposition should be considered as part of the surgical procedure. Some surgeons
recommend routine ulnar neurolysis regardless of preoperative symptoms to prevent
postoperative ulnar nerve irritation.
In patients with concomitant ulnar nerve symptoms, subcutaneous transposition may result
in improved outcomes compared with in situ decompression.20
Surgical option one: longitudinal split and approximation
The flexor origin fascia is divided in line with the muscle fibers just anterior to the medial
raphe.

The enthesis is identified and elevated from the epicondyle.
Diseased tissue is débrided via sharp dissection or by scraping the tissue with the use of the
rounded portion of a No. 15 blade.
The epicondyle can be decorticated or drilled to facilitate tendon-to-bone healing.
The fascia is repaired in a side-to-side manner.
A bone anchor can be used if extensive débridement is performed and direct repair to the
medial epicondyle is considered.
Surgical option two: transverse tendon takedown and reattachment
A three-sided flap is elevated off the medial epicondyle and condyle.
Degenerated and diseased tissue is débrided from the epicondyle and the undersurface of
the elevated tendon.
Two holes are drilled from the epicondyle, exiting the posterior distal humerus.
Nonabsorbable suture is used, either in a horizontal mattress or running locking pattern,
with one limb passed through each drill hole and tied over the bone bridge.
The remaining fascia is reapproximated (Video 3).
The anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament deep to the flexor-pronator is evaluated.
Postoperative management consists of brief immobilization followed by range of motion.
Strengthening is not initiated until 6 weeks postoperatively.

Complications
Infection
Infection is uncommon.
Instability
Overly aggressive débridement or epicondylar resection may result in injury to the underlying
MCL, causing valgus instability.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Ulnar neuropathy from traction or surgical trauma
Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury
Other Complications
Heterotopic ossification may occur.
Rehabilitation
Similar to that for lateral epicondylitis
Outcomes
Case series report notable variation in good or excellent results (63% to 97%) after surgical
management.21-25
Pearls and Pitfalls
Similar to those for lateral epicondylitis.
Correct diagnosis is critical. An understanding of the appropriate physical examination and
appropriate use of imaging studies allows for differentiation of ulnar collateral ligament injury
from medial epicondylitis.
